title: The Witness of Little Hawley
premise: Tamsin Ravensworth, the meticulous archivist of Little Hawley Cathedral, has spent eleven years guarding a locked crypt and an unsolved case: the disappearance of choirgirl Edith Marlowe in 1974. When Edith's diary surfaces in the cathedral archives with entries written years after her disappearance — in handwriting Tamsin slowly realizes matches her own forgotten childhood — she discovers she was the last person to see Edith alive, a memory someone drugged out of her. As Tamsin reopens the case from inside it, the killer, now a beloved pillar of the town who has spent decades editing the record, begins erasing witnesses and documents alike. In the crypt itself, Tamsin traps him using the one thing he cannot edit: the sealed ledger of burials he never knew existed, and Edith is finally found and named.
about_author: E. M. Whitlock is the pen name of a former parish archivist who spent fifteen years cataloguing English cathedral records before turning to crime fiction. They write in the margins of old ledgers and claim every mystery they've ever solved began with a misfiled document.

chapters.title: The Locked Crypt
chapters.summary: Tamsin Ravensworth, POV. Establishes her pride in closed cases as she catalogs the cathedral archive beneath Little Hawley, past the iron gate of the crypt that no key opens. A delivery arrives: a water-damaged diary donated anonymously. Emotional beat: quiet order disrupted by a first crack of unease.

chapters.title: Edith Marlowe, 1974
chapters.summary: Tamsin reads the early diary entries of twelve-year-old Edith, missing for fifty-one years, and cross-references them against the original police file she keeps out of professional habit. The dates stop abruptly on the day Edith vanished. Emotional beat: fascination curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Tamsin finds pages bound deeper in the diary dated 1976, 1980, 1999 — written after the disappearance. The handwriting unsettles her; it looks like her own. Emotional beat: denial, then the first vertigo of self-doubt.

chapters.title: The Dean's Dinner
chapters.summary: Third-person limited through Tamsin at a town dinner where prominent citizens — including solicitor Ambrose Pell, the cathedral's chief benefactor — dismiss talk of reopening old wounds. Someone asks pointed questions about what's kept downstairs. Emotional beat: Tamsin realizes the case has defenders.

chapters.title: What I Cannot Remember
chapters.summary: Tamsin interrogates her own childhood: raised in Little Hawley by an aunt, a two-year gap in her memory around age six. She writes down everything she does recall and finds gaps shaped exactly like Edith's final week. Emotional beat: grief for a self she can't verify.

chapters.title: The Choir Robe
chapters.summary: In a sealed vestry box, Tamsin finds a child's choir robe with initials E.M. and a dark stain the 1974 investigation never logged. Whose POV alternates briefly with a 1974 flashback of Edith hiding something in the vestry. Emotional beat: the past physically touching the present.

chapters.title: A Visitor Who Knows Too Much
chapters.summary: An elderly woman claiming to be Edith's schoolmate visits the archive, steering Tamsin toward a suspect long dead. Afterward Tamsin checks the visitor register — the woman signed a name that appears nowhere in any school record. Emotional beat: the hunter realizing she is being hunted.

chapters.title: The Edited File
chapters.summary: Tamsin compares the police file against newspaper microfilm and finds pages removed, dates altered, a witness statement rewritten in different ink. Someone with archival access has been tending this case for decades. Emotional beat: cold fury — her own domain desecrated.

chapters.title: Ambrose Pell's Kindness
chapters.summary: Pell offers Tamsin funding, discretion, and gently suggests she take leave, citing her 'fragile history.' His knowledge of that history is more precise than any public record allows. Emotional beat: charm revealed as surveillance.

chapters.title: The Diary Continues
chapters.summary: Tamsin decodes Edith's later entries: coded references to 'the gentleman of the ledger' and a threat witnessed in the crypt the night she vanished. One entry describes a frightened child watching from the stairs — described in terms that mirror Tamsin's only surviving fragment of memory. Emotional beat: recognition like a trapdoor opening.

chapters.title: I Was There
chapters.summary: Under hypnosis-adjacent journaling, Tamsin recovers the night: age six, unable to sleep, she saw a man carry something heavy into the crypt and was found wandering, drugged, by the verger — who told her aunt she'd dreamed it. Emotional beat: horror and terrible relief; she wasn't broken, she was silenced.

chapters.title: The Verger's Silence
chapters.summary: The retired verger, dying in a care home, confirms the drugging and names the man whose orders he followed — but dies before saying the name aloud, leaving only a hymn number clutched in his hand. Emotional beat: hope raised and snatched away.

chapters.title: Hymn 174
chapters.summary: Tamsin traces the hymn to its composer and its dedication page in the cathedral's own printed history: dedicated by Ambrose Pell to his father, the cathedral's former sacristan. Emotional beat: the shape of the answer, still unprovable.

chapters.title: Erasure
chapters.summary: Someone breaks into the archive overnight. The diary is gone, the vestry box emptied, and Tamsin's own employment file now contains a fabricated psychiatric history designed to discredit anything she says. Emotional beat: isolation — the record itself turned against her.

chapters.title: Found Family
chapters.summary: Tamsin's chosen people rally: the young bell-ringer Nell, the skeptical police sergeant Okafor who once dismissed her, and the dean's elderly housekeeper each bring fragments. Sergeant Okafor quietly reopens the file off the books. Emotional beat: warmth against the cold — she is not alone with the truth.

chapters.title: The Ledger He Never Read
chapters.summary: Nell finds the cathedral's burial ledger, sealed since 1962 and never digitized or edited: it records an 'irregular interment' in the crypt's disused ossuary niche in October 1974, entered by the elder Pell and countersigned by no one. Emotional beat: triumph — physical evidence outside the killer's reach.

chapters.title: Bait
chapters.summary: Knowing Pell watches the archive, Tamsin lets slip through official channels that the crypt will be unsealed for inspection on a specific morning. She and Okafor prepare the trap, aware he may have a second way in — and that he knows the building better than anyone alive. Emotional beat: controlled terror, the gambler's calm.

chapters.title: The Unsealing
chapters.summary: Inspection day. Pell appears with lawyers and the bishop, all smiles — while, per the plan, the real work happens below. But the crypt gate stands already open, and the ossuary niche has been disturbed within hours. Emotional beat: the trap sprung on both sides at once.

chapters.title: What the Dark Keeps
chapters.summary: Climax part one. Tamsin descends alone, following fresh marks, and confronts Pell among the bones. He confesses with terrible calm — his father killed Edith; he has spent fifty years protecting the family name and editing the world to match. He locks the gate behind them. Emotional beat: face-to-face with the editor of her life.

chapters.title: The Witness Speaks
chapters.summary: Climax part two. Trapped in the dark, Tamsin uses the thing Pell can't edit: her voice, live via the bell-ringers' intercom, narrating his confession to the whole tower above as Nell and Okafor force the gate. Edith's remains are recovered from the niche, folded with dignity — someone once tried, in guilt, to lay her properly. Emotional beat: the silenced child of chapter eleven finally testifying.

chapters.title: Closing the Case
chapters.summary: Aftermath: Pell's empire of quiet revisions unravels as the untouched ledger anchors every other document. Tamsin writes Edith's true final entry in the archive's register, files the case closed in her own hand, and gives the recovered diary a place of honor. Emotional beat: restoration — the record made honest.

chapters.title: The Open Door
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Tamsin's POV. At Edith's memorial service, the town sings hymn 174 without shame, reclaimed. Tamsin leaves the crypt gate unlocked for the first time in fifty years and accepts Nell as her apprentice archivist. Final line echoes the diary: some things kept are meant, at last, to be told. Emotional beat: peace, identity chosen rather than assigned.
